### Frostbite

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Frostbite")]

[Frostbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite "Frostbite") is a cold-related injury occurring when an area (typically a limb or other extremity)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-17) is exposed to extreme low temperatures, causing the freezing of the skin or other tissues.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-handford2017-18) Its [pathophysiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathophysiology "Pathophysiology") involves the formation of ice crystals upon freezing and [blood clots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_clot "Blood clot") upon thawing, leading to [cell damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_damage "Cell damage") and [cell death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_death "Cell death").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-handford2017-18) Treatment of severe frostbite may require surgical amputation of the affected tissue or limb;[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-19) if there is deep injury [autoamputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoamputation "Autoamputation") may occur.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-20)

### Athletic performance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Athletic performance")]

Sometimes professional [athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") may choose to have a non-essential digit amputated to relieve chronic pain and impaired performance.

*   Australian Rules footballer [Daniel Chick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Chick "Daniel Chick") elected to have his left [ring finger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_finger "Ring finger") amputated as chronic pain and injury was limiting his performance.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-21)
*   [Rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union") player [Jone Tawake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jone_Tawake "Jone Tawake") also had a finger removed.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-22)
*   [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League")[safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_(American_and_Canadian_football_position) "Safety (American and Canadian football position)")[Ronnie Lott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Lott "Ronnie Lott") had the tip of his little finger removed after it was damaged in the [1985 NFL season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_NFL_season "1985 NFL season").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-23)

### Criminal penalties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Criminal penalties")]

*   According to [Quran 5:38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran_5:38 "Quran 5:38"), the punishment for stealing is the amputation of the hand. Under [Sharia law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharia_law "Sharia law"), after repeated offense, the foot may also be cut off. This is still in practice today in countries like [Brunei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunei "Brunei"), the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-24)[Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Telegraph_2008-26)[Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-MC_2007-27)[Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-28) and 11 of the 36 states within [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-30)
*   **[Cross-amputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-amputation "Cross-amputation")** is one of the [Hudud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudud "Hudud") punishments prescribed under [Islamic jurisprudence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiqh "Fiqh") (Sharia law) and involves cutting off the right hand and left foot of the alleged transgressor.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-32) The scriptural authority for the double amputation procedure is in the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") (_surah_ 5.33–34) which stipulates:
> The punishment of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger, and strive with might for mischief through the land is execution or crucifixion, or cutting of hands and feet from opposite sides, or exile from the land. As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands and feet from opposite ends in recompense for what they have committed.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-33)

 The severe [punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punishment "Punishment"), for "highway robbery (_[hirabah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirabah "Hirabah")_, _qat' al-tariq_) and civil disturbance against Islam", is usually carried out in a single session in public, without anaesthetic and using a sword. The ancient punishment is practised in Islamic countries such as Saudi Arabia,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-34) Sudan,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-35) Somalia,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-36) Mauritania, the Maldives,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-37) Iran,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-38) Afghanistan (under Taliban rule),[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and Yemen.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-39)
*   In 1779, [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") proposed a bill to the [Virginia Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Assembly "Virginia Assembly") that ostensibly would have replaced [capital punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") with other penalties, including amputation, for certain crimes,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Boyd_TJP-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Wilson_Bill_64-41) although not all were really punishable by death at the time.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-42) For the crimes of rape, sodomy, and polygamy (the last removed from a later version), the punishment was to be [castration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castration "Castration") for men or [rhinotomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhinotomy "Rhinotomy") for women.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-43) For [intentional maiming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayhem_(crime) "Mayhem (crime)"), the bill specified literal [eye for an eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_for_an_eye "Eye for an eye") retribution.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-44) The bill never passed, due to the combination of its perceived barbarity in some parts and perceived leniency in others.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Wilson_Bill_64-41)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-45)
*   In England, the [Offences within the Court Act 1541](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offences_within_the_Court_Act_1541 "Offences within the Court Act 1541") provided for cutting off a hand as punishment for striking someone inside a courtroom. Thomas Jefferson's punishments revision bill also intended to repeal this.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-46) The punishment was abolished in England and Wales by the [Offences Against the Person Act 1828](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offences_Against_the_Person_Act_1828 "Offences Against the Person Act 1828").
*   As of 2021, this form of punishment is controversial, as most modern cultures consider it to be morally abhorrent, as it has the effect of permanently disabling a person and constitutes torture. It is thus seen as grossly disproportionate for crimes less than those such as murder.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-47)

## Surgery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Surgery")]

### Method

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Method")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Curvy_amputation_knife_DSC09451.jpg/250px-Curvy_amputation_knife_DSC09451.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Curvy_amputation_knife_DSC09451.jpg)

Curved knives such as this one were used, in the past, for some kinds of amputations.

Surgeons performing an amputation have to first [ligate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligature_(medicine) "Ligature (medicine)") the supplying [artery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artery "Artery") and [vein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vein "Vein"), so as to prevent [hemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemorrhage "Hemorrhage") (bleeding). The muscles are transected, and finally, the [bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone "Bone") is sawed through with an [oscillating saw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscillating_saw "Oscillating saw"). Sharp and rough edges of bones are filed, and skin and muscle flaps are then transposed over the stump, occasionally with the insertion of elements to attach a [prosthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosthesis "Prosthesis").

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/%C3%9Altimos_momentos_do_heroico_1%C2%BA_tenente_-_Mariz_e_Barros_-_commandante_do_encoura%C3%A7ado_-_Tamandar%C3%A9._-.jpg/250px-%C3%9Altimos_momentos_do_heroico_1%C2%BA_tenente_-_Mariz_e_Barros_-_commandante_do_encoura%C3%A7ado_-_Tamandar%C3%A9._-.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%C3%9Altimos_momentos_do_heroico_1%C2%BA_tenente_-_Mariz_e_Barros_-_commandante_do_encoura%C3%A7ado_-_Tamandar%C3%A9._-.jpg)

Amputation of the leg of First Lieutenant [Antônio Carlos de Mariz e Barros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B4nio_Carlos_de_Mariz_e_Barros "Antônio Carlos de Mariz e Barros"), commander of the Brazilian [Battleship _Tamandaré_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_ironclad_Tamandar%C3%A9 "Brazilian ironclad Tamandaré") (Henrique Fleiuss, _Semana Illustrada_, [1866](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1866 "1866"))

Distal stabilisation of muscles is often performed. This allows effective muscle contraction which reduces atrophy, allows functional use of the stump and maintains soft tissue coverage of the remnant bone. The preferred stabilisation technique is myodesis where the muscle is attached to the bone or its periosteum. In joint disarticulation amputations tenodesis may be used where the muscle tendon is attached to the bone. Muscles are attached under similar tension to normal physiological conditions.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-48)

An experimental technique known as the "Ewing amputation" aims to improve post-amputation [proprioception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proprioception "Proprioception").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-50) Another technique with similar goals, which has been tested in a clinical trial,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-51) is Agonist-antagonist Myoneural Interface (AMI).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-52)

In 1920, Dr. Janos Ertl Sr. of [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary"), developed the Ertl procedure in order to return a high number of amputees to the workforce.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-53) The Ertl technique, an osteomyoplastic procedure for transtibial amputation, can be used to create a highly functional residual limb. Creation of a tibiofibular bone bridge provides a stable, broad tibiofibular articulation that may be capable of some distal weight bearing. Several different modified techniques and fibular bridge fixation methods have been used; however, no current evidence exists regarding comparison of the different techniques.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-54)

### Post-operative management

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Post-operative management")]

A 2019 [Cochrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochrane_(organisation) "Cochrane (organisation)")[systematic review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematic_review "Systematic review") aimed to determine whether rigid dressings were more effective than soft dressings in helping wounds heal following transtibial (below the knee) amputations. Due to the limited and very low certainty of evidence available, the authors concluded that it was uncertain what the benefits and harms were for each dressing type. They recommended that clinicians consider the pros and cons of each dressing type on a case-by-case basis: rigid dressings may potentially benefit patients who have a high risk of falls; soft dressings may potentially benefit patients who have poor skin integrity.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-55)

A 2017 review found that the use of rigid removable dressings (RRD's) in trans-tibial amputations, rather than soft bandaging, improved healing time, reduced edema, prevented knee flexion contractures and reduced complications, including further amputation, from external trauma such as falls onto the stump.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-56)

Post-operative management, in addition to wound healing, considers maintenance of limb strength, joint range, edema management, preservation of the intact limb (if applicable) and stump desensitization.

## Trauma

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Trauma")]

Traumatic amputation is the partial or total avulsion of a part of a body during a serious accident, like traffic, labor, or combat.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Watson1986-58)

Traumatic amputation of a human limb, either partial or total, creates the immediate danger of death from blood loss.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-59)

Orthopedic surgeons often assess the severity of different injuries using the Mangled Extremity Severity Score. Given different clinical and situational factors, they can predict the likelihood of amputation. This is especially useful for emergency physicians to quickly evaluate patients and decide on consultations.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-60)

### Causes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Causes")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/3372709503_10dc75d783_oS%C3%A9quelleAmputation.jpg/250px-3372709503_10dc75d783_oS%C3%A9quelleAmputation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:3372709503_10dc75d783_oS%C3%A9quelleAmputation.jpg)

Private Lewis Francis was wounded July 21, 1861, at the [First Battle of Bull Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Bull_Run "First Battle of Bull Run") by a bayonet to the knee.

Traumatic amputation is uncommon in humans (1 per 20,804 population per year). Loss of limb usually happens immediately during the accident, but sometimes a few days later after medical complications. Statistically, the most common causes of traumatic amputations are:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-61)

*   Vehicle accidents (cars, motorcycles, bicycles, trains, etc.)
*   Labor accidents (equipment, instruments, cylinders, chainsaws, press machines, meat machines, wood machines, etc.)
*   Agricultural accidents, with machines and mower equipment
*   Electric shock hazards
*   Firearms, bladed weapons, explosives
*   Violent rupture of ship rope or industry wire rope
*   Ring traction (ring amputation, de-gloving injuries)
*   Building doors and car doors
*   Animal attacks
*   Gas cylinder explosions[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-62)
*   Other rare accidents[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-63)

### Treatment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Treatment")]

The development of the science of [microsurgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsurgery "Microsurgery") over the last 40 years has provided several treatment options for a traumatic amputation, depending on the patient's specific trauma and clinical situation:[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-64)

*   1st choice: Surgical amputation - break - prosthesis
*   2nd choice: Surgical amputation - transplantation of other tissue - plastic reconstruction.
*   3rd choice: [Replantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replantation "Replantation") - reconnection - revascularisation of amputated limb, by microscope (after 1969)
*   4th choice: Transplantation of cadaveric hand (after 2000)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Watson1986-58)

### Epidemiology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Epidemiology")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/In_Khmelnytskyi%2C_the_President_Paid_a_Visit_to_the_Warriors_Recovering_from_Wounds_and_Presented_Them_with_Awards._%2853698029200%29.jpg/250px-In_Khmelnytskyi%2C_the_President_Paid_a_Visit_to_the_Warriors_Recovering_from_Wounds_and_Presented_Them_with_Awards._%2853698029200%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:In_Khmelnytskyi,_the_President_Paid_a_Visit_to_the_Warriors_Recovering_from_Wounds_and_Presented_Them_with_Awards._(53698029200).jpg)

Up to 50,000 Ukrainians lost their limbs during the [Russo-Ukrainian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022%E2%80%93present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-65)

*   In the United States in 1999, there were 14,420 non-fatal traumatic amputations according to the [American Statistical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Statistical_Association "American Statistical Association"). Of these, 4,435 occurred as a result of traffic and transportation accidents and 9,985 were due to labor accidents. Of all traumatic amputations, the distribution percentage is 30.75% for traffic accidents and 69.24% for labor accidents.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-amstat.org-66)[_[not specific enough to verify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]
*   The United States Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 6,200 cases of work-related amputations in 2018. The most common causes of amputations were machinery (58% cases), crush injuries from parts or material (15%), and other tools/instruments/equipment such hand tools (7%).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-67)
*   A study found that in 2010, 22.8% of patients undergoing amputation of a lower extremity in the United States were readmitted to the hospital within 30 days.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-68)
*   In 2017, an estimated 57.7 million people globally were living with existing traumatic limb injuries. Of these 57.7 million, the leading causes of amputation "were falls (36.2%), road injuries (15.7%), other transportation injuries (11.2%), and mechanical forces (10.4%)."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-69)
*   On 2 August 2023, an investigation by _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ found that Ukrainian medical amputations in the war came to between 20,000 and 50,000 including both military and civilians. In comparison, during [World War One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_One "World War One") 41,000 British and 67,000 Germans needed amputations.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-70)
*   In 2025, Israel's [attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_war_crimes_in_the_Gaza_war "Israeli war crimes in the Gaza war") on the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip") during the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") caused Gaza to have the highest number of [child amputees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_of_the_Gaza_war_on_children_in_the_Gaza_Strip "Effect of the Gaza war on children in the Gaza Strip") per capita in the world.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-72)

## Prevention

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Prevention")]

Methods in preventing amputation, [limb-sparing techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limb-sparing_techniques "Limb-sparing techniques"), depend on the problems that might cause amputations to be necessary. Chronic infections, often caused by diabetes or [decubitus ulcers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decubitus_ulcers "Decubitus ulcers") in bedridden patients, are common causes of infections that lead to gangrene, which, when widespread, necessitates amputation.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-73)

There are two key challenges: first, many patients have impaired circulation in their extremities, and second, they have difficulty curing infections in limbs with poor blood circulation.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-75)

Crush injuries where there is extensive tissue damage and poor circulation also benefit from [hyperbaric oxygen therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbaric_medicine "Hyperbaric medicine") (HBOT). The high level of oxygenation and revascularization speed up recovery times and prevent infections.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-76)

A study found that the patented method called Circulator Boot achieved significant results in prevention of amputation in patients with diabetes and arteriosclerosis.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-dillon1-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-dillon2-78) Another study found it also effective for healing limb ulcers caused by peripheral vascular disease.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-vella-79) The boot checks the heart rhythm and compresses the limb between heartbeats; the compression helps cure the wounds in the walls of veins and arteries, and helps to push the blood back to the heart.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-80)

For victims of trauma, advances in [microsurgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsurgery "Microsurgery") in the 1970s have made replantation of severed body parts possible.

The establishment of laws, rules, and guidelines, and the employment of modern equipment help protect people from traumatic amputations.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-81)

## Prognosis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Prognosis")]

The individual may experience psychological trauma and emotional discomfort. The stump will remain an area of reduced mechanical stability. Limb loss can present significant or even drastic practical limitations.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Amputation-82)

A large proportion of amputees (from 50 to 80% to 80–100%, according to different studies) experience the phenomenon of [phantom limbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_limb "Phantom limb");[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-PhantomReview2007-84) they feel body parts that are no longer there. These limbs can itch, ache, burn, feel tense, dry or wet, locked in or trapped or they can feel as if they are moving. Some scientists believe it has to do with a kind of neural map that the brain has of the body, which sends information to the rest of the brain about limbs regardless of their existence. Phantom sensations and [phantom pain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_pain "Phantom pain") may also occur after the removal of body parts other than the limbs, e.g. after amputation of the breast, extraction of a tooth (phantom tooth pain) or removal of an eye ([phantom eye syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_eye_syndrome "Phantom eye syndrome")).

A similar phenomenon is an unexplained sensation in a body part unrelated to the amputated limb. It has been hypothesized that the portion of the brain responsible for processing stimulation from amputated limbs, being deprived of input, expands into the surrounding brain, (_[Phantoms in the Brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantoms\_in\_the\_Brain "Phantoms in the Brain")_: [V.S. Ramachandran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V.S._Ramachandran "V.S. Ramachandran") and [Sandra Blakeslee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandra_Blakeslee "Sandra Blakeslee")) such that an individual who has had an arm amputated will experience unexplained pressure or movement on his face or head.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-85)

In many cases, the phantom limb aids in adaptation to a prosthesis, as it permits the person to experience [proprioception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proprioception "Proprioception") of the prosthetic limb. To support improved resistance or usability, comfort or healing, some types of [stump socks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stump_sock "Stump sock") may be worn instead of or as part of wearing a prosthesis.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-Amputation-82)

Another side effect can be [heterotopic ossification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterotopic_ossification "Heterotopic ossification"), especially when a bone injury is combined with a head injury. The brain signals the bone to grow instead of scar tissue to form, and nodules and other growth can interfere with prosthetics and sometimes require further operations. This type of injury has been especially common among soldiers wounded by [improvised explosive devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvised_explosive_device "Improvised explosive device") in the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-86)

Due to technological advances in prosthetics, many amputees live active lives with little restriction. Organizations such as the [Challenged Athletes Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenged_Athletes_Foundation "Challenged Athletes Foundation") have been developed to give amputees the opportunity to be involved in athletics and [adaptive sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_sports "Adaptive sports") such as [amputee soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee_football "Amputee football").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-87)

Nearly half of the individuals who have an amputation due to vascular disease will die within 5 years, usually secondary to the extensive co-morbidities rather than due to direct consequences of an amputation. This is higher than the five year mortality rates for breast cancer, colon cancer, and prostate cancer.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-88) Of persons with diabetes who have a lower extremity amputation, up to 55% will require amputation of the second leg within two to three years.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-89)

## Medieval and early modern Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Medieval and early modern Europe")]

Amputations in medieval and early modern Europe were mainly the result of warfare, disease, work accidents, and punishment. Amputations were performed by [barber-surgeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barber_surgeon "Barber surgeon").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:3-90)

### Disease

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Disease")]

One of the major causes of amputation in medieval Europe was disease. [Ergotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergotism "Ergotism") (also known as Saint-Anthony's fire) was a fungus found in rye that caused gangrene that spread from the fingers and toes. If the tissue death from the disease was severe enough, the limb would spontaneously fall off on its own without blood loss.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-91)

### Warfare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Warfare")]

Warfare amputations became more necessary in Europe after European armies started using guns in the fourteenth century. At the time, bullet wounds were often too complicated for surgeons to handle, and amputation was their best solution.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-92) In the late fifteenth century, we see more documentation of amputations as [Hieronymus Brunschwig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_Brunschwig "Hieronymus Brunschwig") and [Hans Von Gersdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_von_Gersdorff "Hans von Gersdorff") both illustrated amputation scenes, with the latter also writing about gunshot injuries.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-93) Gersdorff's writings showed that surgeons at the time struggled with whether the gunpowder on the wound further worsened the injuries. Therefore, it was a common practice to cauterize the wounds with hot oil until [Ambroise Paré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambroise_Par%C3%A9 "Ambroise Paré") discovered that this impeded healing, and concluded that gunshot wounds should not be cauterized. This led to another significant contribution of his to warfare medicine: the revival of [ligature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligature_(medicine) "Ligature (medicine)"), which replaced cauterization of amputation wounds. Paré updated ligature to make it safer, and it became common practice.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-94)

### Amputation as punishment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Amputation as punishment")]

There is evidence of amputation as punishment dating back to 1750 BCE. The Babylonian Code of [King Hammurabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammurabi "Hammurabi") sanctioned amputation as a punishment. Amputation as a punishment continued in ancient [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"), where the part of the body amputated had a connection to the crime committed (for example, stealing might be punished by amputating the hand of the guilty). Amputation continued as a form of punishment into the Roman period as well as the Byzantine period, but became less prominent after the collapse of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"). These punishments increased again during the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), but declined again after perceptions of punitive amputation changed significantly during the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") and [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-95)

In medieval Europe, corpses would sometimes be amputated after death as a form of public shaming or punishment.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-96)[Medieval Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_the_Middle_Ages "Christianity in the Middle Ages") believed strongly in the importance of bodily integrity, even after death; therefore, post-execution dismemberment reflected the expectation of eternal damnation for the worst criminals.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-97)

There is also documentation of nose amputation being used as a form of punishment or retaliation. In [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") during the 5th and 6th centuries, nose cutting was prominent enough to be classified as its own crime, which would result in a serious fine to the perpetrator. However, it was also occasionally used as a punishment for serious crimes such as threatening royals.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-98) The field of [plastic surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_surgery "Plastic surgery") was brought to Europe, specifically [Catania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catania "Catania"), in the fifteenth century, when Gustavo Branca successfully completed an ancient Indian method of reconstructive [rhinoplasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhinoplasty "Rhinoplasty"). Plastic surgery continued to grow as a field across the continent, and the birth of this field is likely related to nose amputation as punishment.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-99)

### Theories on amputation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Theories on amputation")]

In medieval Europe, amputation was done on limbs as a last resort when the limb could not be saved. For limbs that were dead or decaying, surgeons categorized them into two main categories: hot fire and cold fire. Hot fire (also called Gangraena) was the first stage of a decaying limb. A body part with hot fire was hot, swollen, and painful. If not treated, the limb would turn cold. Cold fire (also called Sphacelus) was the late stage of limb death, including death of the bone. Symptoms included loss of feeling, coldness, and black and blue coloring. With time, the fire would spread and eventually kill the patient.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:0-100)

Followers of [Galen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galen "Galen") considered hot and cold fire to be based on the humors and an imbalance of hot, wet, dry, and cold in the body. Followers of [Paracelsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsus "Paracelsus") believed that hot and cold fire were a result of Mercury, sulfur, and salt. While different surgeons drew from different medical theories of the time, they also used their own experiences to determine the root cause of the fires. There was often debate on whether a particular patient had cold or hot fire, which led to disagreements on treatment methods.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:0-100)

Treatment for hot fire often included burning or cutting out damaged flesh. If the symptoms were mild enough, the skin could sometimes be regrown. Treatment for cold fire included removing the dead flesh and likely amputation.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:0-100)

### Amputation methods

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Amputation methods")]

Throughout Europe, there were varying approaches when it came to amputations. The two main considerations for amputation procedures were how fast it could be performed and how it would heal. The mallet-and-wedge technique involved setting the body part on a wedge and hitting the wedge with a mallet. This separated the limb or digit from the body by crushing it. This method was very fast but left a messy result that caused the crushed bones to splinter into the remaining part of the limb. The hand's-width method used a curved knife to cut through the limb's tissue, and a bow-frame saw to cut through the bone. An assistant would pull the flesh upwards to expose the bone. After the limb was sawed off, the flesh would then be pulled back over the stump to create a cushion. This procedure took longer but healed more easily.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:1-101)

One method to stop hemorrhaging after amputation was iron [cautery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauterization "Cauterization"). This involved taking hot iron instruments to the new stump and burning off the exposed tissue, closing the blood vessels. Another method of cauterization was to apply corrosive chemicals to the fresh wound to burn the blood vessels and stop the bleeding. Both methods were efficient but led to a long healing process. A different method was [ligation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligature_(medicine) "Ligature (medicine)"). This technique required the surgeon to draw out the individual blood vessels and tie them shut. This process was much more time-consuming but healed more quickly.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:1-101)

There was also debate among barber-surgeons on the location of amputation. One rationale was to amputate as close to the damage as possible to save as much of the remaining limb as possible. Others argued to amputate in a location that would fit a prosthetic the best. This was especially debated for lower leg amputation because a prosthetic would fit better if the leg was amputated closer to the knee.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:1-101) Paré is the first known surgeon to decide the location of an amputation based on how a prosthetic would fit on it in 1564.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:3-90)

### Prosthetics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Prosthetics")]

Prosthetics in the early modern period were made from wood, metal, and leather. The majority of prosthetic artifacts from the period still around today were made of metal. In Germany, metal mechanical hands were made with ratchets and springs. The springs allowed for movement of the fingers, while the ratchets locked them in place. The wearer was able to control the fingers by releasing the ratchets through buttons or levers, depending on the hand. The specific mechanics of the hand varied by prosthetic.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:2-102)

Mechanical prosthetics were the work of artisans, specifically locksmiths and clockmakers. This was because locksmiths and clockmakers were already using springs and ratchets to make locks, doors, and clocks.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-:2-102)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amputation&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The word amputation is borrowed from Latin _amputātus,_ past participle of _amputāre_ "to prune back (a plant), prune away, remove by cutting (unwanted parts or features), cut off (a branch, limb, body part)," from _am-,_ assimilated variant of _amb-_ "about, around" + _putāre_ "to prune, make clean or tidy, scour (wool)". The English word "Poes" was first applied to surgery in the 17th century, possibly first in Peter Lowe's _A discourse of the Whole Art of Chirurgerie_ (published in either 1597 or 1612); his work was derived from 16th-century French texts and early English writers also used the words "extirpation" (16th-century French texts tended to use _extirper_), "[disarticulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disarticulation "Disarticulation")", and "[dismemberment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dismemberment "Dismemberment")" (from the Old French _desmembrer_ and a more common term before the 17th century for limb loss or removal), or simply "cutting", but by the end of the 17th century "amputation" had come to dominate as the accepted medical term.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amputee#cite_note-103)

**Osowiec Fortress** ([Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language"): _Twierdza Osowiec_; [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Крепость Осовец, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian "Romanization of Russian"):_Krepost' Osovets_) is a 19th-century fortress built by the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire"), located in what is now north-eastern [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland"). It saw heavy fighting during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") when it was defended for several months by its Russian garrison against German attacks.

The fortress was built in the years 1882–1892 as one of the defensive works to protect the western borders of Russia against [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire"), and continuously modernised afterwards to cope with advances in heavy siege artillery. In 1889–1893, military engineer [Nestor Buinitsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestor_Buinitsky "Nestor Buinitsky") took an important part in the creation of the fortress. It was located on the river [Biebrza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biebrza "Biebrza") about 50 km from the border with the German province of [East Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Prussia "East Prussia"), in the one place where the marshlands of the river could be crossed, hence controlling a vital chokepoint. The extensive marshlands and bogs that surrounded it made attacks upon it difficult. The strategic [Belostok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belostok "Belostok")–[Lyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyck "Lyck")–[Königsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nigsberg "Königsberg") rail line also ran through the fortress and crossed the Biebrza river there. The fortress saw heavy fighting during the beginning of [World War I in the eastern front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_I) "Eastern Front (World War I)") from September 1914 until the Russian Army abandoned it in August 1915. In the interwar years the fortress was used by the Polish Army. During the [German invasion of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_Poland "German invasion of Poland") in 1939 it was bypassed and did not see much fighting.

Today, some parts of the fortress are accessible to tourists, especially the parts within the boundaries of [Biebrza National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biebrza_National_Park "Biebrza National Park"). The visitor information center of the park is located in [Osowiec-Twierdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec-Twierdza "Osowiec-Twierdza"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-lplanet-1) a small settlement located within the boundaries of the fortress. Other parts of the fortress still belong to the [Polish Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Army "Polish Army") and access is restricted.

## First World War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: First World War")]

### First German assault (September 1914)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: First German assault (September 1914)")]

In September 1914, Russian field defenses surrounding the fortress were attacked by 40 infantry battalions of the German 8th Army; the attackers enjoyed significant numerical superiority. By 21 September, the German advance brought the fortress proper within range of German artillery; further reinforced with 60 additional guns of calibres up to 203mm, but these could only be brought into action on 26 September. On the same day, the city was attacked, 8,000 garrison repelled the attack of 12,000 German army, losing 139 people, German losses up to 6,000.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorisyuk202474%E2%80%9375-2) Two days later, a German frontal assault was repelled by Russian artillery. The day afterwards, two Russian flanking counter-attacks forced German artillery to relocate, taking the fortress outside of German artillery range.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-pb-4)

### Second battle (February–March 1915)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Second battle (February–March 1915)")]

Attempting to cut the railway line between [Białystok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bia%C5%82ystok "Białystok") and Warsaw, the Germans attacked the Osowiec fortress, which was lightly defended by a few Russian battalions. Two days of heavy bombardment by the Germans commenced on 14 February, followed by a second bombardment during the last week of the month. However, German infantry attacks were repelled, and the situation devolved into positional warfare for the next several months.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-PB2-5)

It is sometimes incorrectly claimed that Russian [counter-battery fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-battery_fire "Counter-battery fire") destroyed two German [heavy mortars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bertha_(howitzer) "Big Bertha (howitzer)"); these guns were withdrawn for operations elsewhere.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-kauffman_112-6)

### Third battle (July–August 1915)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Third battle (July–August 1915)")]

Main article: [Attack of the Dead Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_of_the_Dead_Men "Attack of the Dead Men")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Praporshhik_i_podporuchik_kotlinskij_3.jpg/250px-Praporshhik_i_podporuchik_kotlinskij_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Praporshhik_i_podporuchik_kotlinskij_3.jpg)

Lieutenant [Vladimir Karpovich Kotlinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Karpovich_Kotlinsky "Vladimir Karpovich Kotlinsky"), commandant of the Osowiec fortress during the attack

The Germans launched a full frontal offensive on the fortress at the beginning of July; the attack included 14 battalions of infantry, one battalion of sappers, 24–30 heavy siege guns, and 30 batteries of artillery equipped with poison gases led by [Field Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalfeldmarschall "Generalfeldmarschall")[Paul von Hindenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_von_Hindenburg "Paul von Hindenburg"). Russian defences were manned by 500 soldiers of the 226th Infantry Regiment Zemlyansky, and 400 militia.

The Germans knew the Russians did not have any gas masks so they chose to use chlorine gas. The Germans waited until 04:00 on 6 August for favourable wind conditions, when the attack opened with regular artillery bombardment combined with chlorine gas.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-7) The ensuing battle was known as the [Attack of the Dead Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_of_the_Dead_Men "Attack of the Dead Men"). The Russians put on wet rags on their faces to filter some of the gas. Most died but approximately one hundred men survived the gas attack. Even while suffering severe chemical burns the Russians were able to repel the attack due to German forces panicking at the sight of the Russian men, covered in blisters and coughing up bits of their lungs, with the Germans subsequently retreating. The Russian garrison suffered heavy losses, but some soldiers survived even after the final charge, and chlorine gas barrage. This offensive by the remaining Russian troops was dubbed the "Attack of the Dead Men", as the near deceased soldiers resembled the undead, still charging despite being badly injured.

The Russians did not hold Osowiec for much longer. The Germans threatened to encircle the fortress with the capture of [Kaunas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kaunas_(1915) "Siege of Kaunas (1915)") and [Novogeorgiesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Novogeorgievsk "Siege of Novogeorgievsk"). The Russians demolished much of Osowiec and withdrew on 18 August.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-kauffman_112-6)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-kauffman_225-8)

## Second World War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Second World War")]

After the First World War, the [Second Polish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Polish_Republic "Second Polish Republic") refurbished parts of Osowiec and used it to house Polish army units, including the Central School of Non-Commissioned Officers of the [Border Protection Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Protection_Corps "Border Protection Corps").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-Worona-9)

The 135th Reserve Infantry Regiment was formed from the school after Germany [invaded Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland "Invasion of Poland") at the beginning of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). The Poles abandoned the fortress on 13 September. The Germans captured it and passed it to the Soviet 20th Motor Rifle and Machine Gun Brigade on 25 September. Osowiec was subsequently garrisoned by the Soviet [10th Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10th_Army_(Soviet_Union) "10th Army (Soviet Union)"). The Germans recaptured Osowiec on 27 June 1941 during [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa"); one use of the fortress was as an [ammunition dump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammunition_dump "Ammunition dump") there. On 14 August 1944, the Soviet [49th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_Army "49th Army") and [50th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_Army_(Soviet_Union) "50th Army (Soviet Union)") Armies captured three of the forts during the [Osovets Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osovets_Offensive "Osovets Offensive") of [Operation Bagration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Bagration "Operation Bagration"). Fort II remained in German hands until January 1945, when it was abandoned during the [Vistula–Oder Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vistula%E2%80%93Oder_Offensive "Vistula–Oder Offensive").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-Worona-9)

## Post-war

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-war")]

In 1953, the fortress was regarrisoned by a [Polish Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Air_Force "Polish Air Force") ammunition depot,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-Worona-9) which was absorbed into the 11th Regional Materiel Base in 1998.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-10) In 2011, the Osowiec garrison became part of the 2nd Regional Logistics Base.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-11)

I'm writing a paper on war, art, and memory. Specifically, looking at artists who were censored or had their pieces destroyed due to the effects of war and political persecution. I'd like to analyze the work of some current artists who are related to honoring the work of these past artists. There's an award for an artist who lived in what later became part of the Eastern Bloc, who had their work destroyed. I can't remember their name. I know one of their students helped reconstruct some of their pieces and identify other work that had been misattributed to other artists. Also, they were married to a Polish artist who was an amputee and participated in a battle where the Germans thought zombies were attacking them. Could you list the artists who've won the award that honors this past artist? Only list those who've won before 2021.

**Osowiec Fortress** ([Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language"): _Twierdza Osowiec_; [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Крепость Осовец, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian "Romanization of Russian"):_Krepost' Osovets_) is a 19th-century fortress built by the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire"), located in what is now north-eastern [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland"). It saw heavy fighting during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") when it was defended for several months by its Russian garrison against German attacks.

The fortress was built in the years 1882–1892 as one of the defensive works to protect the western borders of Russia against [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire"), and continuously modernised afterwards to cope with advances in heavy siege artillery. In 1889–1893, military engineer [Nestor Buinitsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestor_Buinitsky "Nestor Buinitsky") took an important part in the creation of the fortress. It was located on the river [Biebrza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biebrza "Biebrza") about 50 km from the border with the German province of [East Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Prussia "East Prussia"), in the one place where the marshlands of the river could be crossed, hence controlling a vital chokepoint. The extensive marshlands and bogs that surrounded it made attacks upon it difficult. The strategic [Belostok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belostok "Belostok")–[Lyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyck "Lyck")–[Königsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nigsberg "Königsberg") rail line also ran through the fortress and crossed the Biebrza river there. The fortress saw heavy fighting during the beginning of [World War I in the eastern front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_I) "Eastern Front (World War I)") from September 1914 until the Russian Army abandoned it in August 1915. In the interwar years the fortress was used by the Polish Army. During the [German invasion of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_Poland "German invasion of Poland") in 1939 it was bypassed and did not see much fighting.

Today, some parts of the fortress are accessible to tourists, especially the parts within the boundaries of [Biebrza National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biebrza_National_Park "Biebrza National Park"). The visitor information center of the park is located in [Osowiec-Twierdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec-Twierdza "Osowiec-Twierdza"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-lplanet-1) a small settlement located within the boundaries of the fortress. Other parts of the fortress still belong to the [Polish Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Army "Polish Army") and access is restricted.

## First World War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: First World War")]

### First German assault (September 1914)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: First German assault (September 1914)")]

In September 1914, Russian field defenses surrounding the fortress were attacked by 40 infantry battalions of the German 8th Army; the attackers enjoyed significant numerical superiority. By 21 September, the German advance brought the fortress proper within range of German artillery; further reinforced with 60 additional guns of calibres up to 203mm, but these could only be brought into action on 26 September. On the same day, the city was attacked, 8,000 garrison repelled the attack of 12,000 German army, losing 139 people, German losses up to 6,000.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorisyuk202474%E2%80%9375-2) Two days later, a German frontal assault was repelled by Russian artillery. The day afterwards, two Russian flanking counter-attacks forced German artillery to relocate, taking the fortress outside of German artillery range.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-pb-4)

### Second battle (February–March 1915)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Second battle (February–March 1915)")]

Attempting to cut the railway line between [Białystok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bia%C5%82ystok "Białystok") and Warsaw, the Germans attacked the Osowiec fortress, which was lightly defended by a few Russian battalions. Two days of heavy bombardment by the Germans commenced on 14 February, followed by a second bombardment during the last week of the month. However, German infantry attacks were repelled, and the situation devolved into positional warfare for the next several months.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-PB2-5)

It is sometimes incorrectly claimed that Russian [counter-battery fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-battery_fire "Counter-battery fire") destroyed two German [heavy mortars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bertha_(howitzer) "Big Bertha (howitzer)"); these guns were withdrawn for operations elsewhere.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-kauffman_112-6)

The Germans launched a full frontal offensive on the fortress at the beginning of July; the attack included 14 battalions of infantry, one battalion of sappers, 24–30 heavy siege guns, and 30 batteries of artillery equipped with poison gases led by [Field Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalfeldmarschall "Generalfeldmarschall")[Paul von Hindenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_von_Hindenburg "Paul von Hindenburg"). Russian defences were manned by 500 soldiers of the 226th Infantry Regiment Zemlyansky, and 400 militia.

The Germans knew the Russians did not have any gas masks so they chose to use chlorine gas. The Germans waited until 04:00 on 6 August for favourable wind conditions, when the attack opened with regular artillery bombardment combined with chlorine gas.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-7) The ensuing battle was known as the [Attack of the Dead Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_of_the_Dead_Men "Attack of the Dead Men"). The Russians put on wet rags on their faces to filter some of the gas. Most died but approximately one hundred men survived the gas attack. Even while suffering severe chemical burns the Russians were able to repel the attack due to German forces panicking at the sight of the Russian men, covered in blisters and coughing up bits of their lungs, with the Germans subsequently retreating. The Russian garrison suffered heavy losses, but some soldiers survived even after the final charge, and chlorine gas barrage. This offensive by the remaining Russian troops was dubbed the "Attack of the Dead Men", as the near deceased soldiers resembled the undead, still charging despite being badly injured.

The Russians did not hold Osowiec for much longer. The Germans threatened to encircle the fortress with the capture of [Kaunas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kaunas_(1915) "Siege of Kaunas (1915)") and [Novogeorgiesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Novogeorgievsk "Siege of Novogeorgievsk"). The Russians demolished much of Osowiec and withdrew on 18 August.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-kauffman_112-6)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-kauffman_225-8)

## Second World War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Second World War")]

After the First World War, the [Second Polish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Polish_Republic "Second Polish Republic") refurbished parts of Osowiec and used it to house Polish army units, including the Central School of Non-Commissioned Officers of the [Border Protection Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Protection_Corps "Border Protection Corps").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-Worona-9)

The 135th Reserve Infantry Regiment was formed from the school after Germany [invaded Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland "Invasion of Poland") at the beginning of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). The Poles abandoned the fortress on 13 September. The Germans captured it and passed it to the Soviet 20th Motor Rifle and Machine Gun Brigade on 25 September. Osowiec was subsequently garrisoned by the Soviet [10th Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10th_Army_(Soviet_Union) "10th Army (Soviet Union)"). The Germans recaptured Osowiec on 27 June 1941 during [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa"); one use of the fortress was as an [ammunition dump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammunition_dump "Ammunition dump") there. On 14 August 1944, the Soviet [49th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_Army "49th Army") and [50th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_Army_(Soviet_Union) "50th Army (Soviet Union)") Armies captured three of the forts during the [Osovets Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osovets_Offensive "Osovets Offensive") of [Operation Bagration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Bagration "Operation Bagration"). Fort II remained in German hands until January 1945, when it was abandoned during the [Vistula–Oder Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vistula%E2%80%93Oder_Offensive "Vistula–Oder Offensive").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-Worona-9)

## Post-war

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Osowiec_Fortress&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-war")]

In 1953, the fortress was regarrisoned by a [Polish Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Air_Force "Polish Air Force") ammunition depot,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-Worona-9) which was absorbed into the 11th Regional Materiel Base in 1998.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-10) In 2011, the Osowiec garrison became part of the 2nd Regional Logistics Base.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osowiec_Fortress#cite_note-11)
